rationale: The student says "b is tied to a" and that when a becomes 7, b becomes 7 too, showing they believe assignment keeps variables linked rather than binding b to the value object at that time.

The student says "other and nums are connected after other = nums" and that "whatever other gets, nums gets as well," showing they believe assignment creates a persistent link so reassigning other changes nums.
The student says "x = y means x passes its value over to y," treating assignment as copying from left to right and concluding y becomes 10 while x stays 10.
The student says "b = a gives b's 3 to a," treating assignment as copying from left to right instead of binding b to a's value.

The student states "b = a makes b its own copy of the list, so appending to b does not affect a," treating assignment as copying the list into an independent object rather than binding b to the same list.

The student says the function receives "a copy of data called items" and that appending to that copy leaves the outside `data` empty, which is the misconception that passing a list creates an independent copy.
The student says f “prints 3, and that's what it gives back,” treating the printed value as the function’s return value and assigning it to y.
The student says "returning shows the number on the screen," treating return as displaying output rather than merely handing a value back to the caller.
The student says that because x is passed in as n, increasing n inside bump means x goes up by one. This treats the parameter as linked to the caller's variable.
The student says "since n is x, x is 6 now too," treating the parameter n as linked to the caller's variable x so that reassigning n inside the function changes x.
The student says the program first “hits greet, which prints hi,” even though greet is only defined and never called, showing they think the function body runs when the def is reached.
The student says the print inside show happens first because Python reads top to bottom, treating the function body as executing when the def is reached, before the later call.
The student says that after calling make(), secret is 42 and can be printed, treating a variable assigned inside the function as still existing in the caller after the call ends.
The student says "value is still 3 from inside the function" after the call, treating the local variable `value` as if it continues to exist outside the function frame.

The student says the function "returns n but keeps going to the next line and prints after," treating the print below the return as executing, which is exactly the belief that execution continues past return.

The student says "5 is positive so it hits return pos, but then the last line also runs and returns non-pos, which replaces it," treating execution as continuing past the first return so a later return overrides it.

The student correctly treats n as a local name in bump's frame, says `n = n + 1` only rebinds n to 6, and that x outside still refers to 5 — accurate notional-machine reasoning with no catalog misconceptions.

The student correctly distinguishes print from return: "f prints 3 but has no return, so it gives back None," and binds that returned value to y. This is accurate notional-machine reasoning with no catalog misconception.

The student correctly says "a and b are two names for the same list," so appending through b affects the same object printed via a. This reflects correct aliasing reasoning, not a listed misconception.

The student explains that `secret` exists only during the call to `make()` and disappears once the call returns, so `print(secret)` raises an error. This is correct notional-machine reasoning about local frames, showing no misconception.
The student states that "def just defines greet, it never gets called, so only start shows," which is correct notional-machine reasoning: defining a function does not execute its body.
The student says "honestly I'm not sure, I just multiplied by 3," which only describes a guess at the arithmetic and gives no account of how the call, assignment, or return execute.

The student expects `value` to still be available after `setup()` returns and prints as 3, showing locals outlive the call. They also say "returning also shows the value," treating return as displaying output.

The student says "append adds a 1," which shows minimal but recognizable reasoning that the append operation adds 1 to the list. It does not reveal any of the listed misconceptions about assignment, parameters, return, or frames.
The student says "bump kinda changes it so 6," indicating they believe calling bump(x) changes the caller's variable x through the parameter n.
The student says "y is 3 bc f printed it," treating the value displayed by print inside f as the value handed back to the caller and bound to y. This conflates printing with returning.
The student says "other and nums are the same thing after that line," indicating they believe `other = nums` keeps the variables linked so reassigning `other` to `[9]` also changes `nums`.

The student predicts print(secret) succeeds because "make sets it," treating the local name secret created inside the call as still available in the caller after make() returns, showing no notion of the frame disappearing.
The student expects "after" to print even though it follows `return n`, saying "that line is still in check," i.e. the body keeps executing past the return statement.
The student says "greet prints hi doesnt it" even though greet is only defined and never called, showing they expect the function body to run when the def is reached.
The student says "items is like its own list now," treating the parameter as an independent copy of the passed list, so the append inside add wouldn't be visible in data — hence predicting [].
The student says "x goes into y" for `x = y`, treating assignment as copying from left to right and predicting both values become 10.
The student says "x was tripled" and predicts x becomes 6, showing they believe reassigning the parameter n inside triple changes the caller's variable x.

The student expects 8 to appear in the output, saying "returning 8 puts it out," treating the return value from double(4) as something displayed on screen rather than a value handed back to the caller.

The student predicts "non-pos" and justifies it with "it ends at the bottom return," treating the later return as the one that takes effect even though the earlier `return "pos"` should end the call immediately.
The student says "b follows a" and predicts b becomes 7 after a is reassigned, showing they think b = a keeps b linked to a rather than binding b to the current value of a.
The student says "n is only inside the function," indicating they understand n is local to the function and does not affect x, so the prediction 5 is correct.

The student says "f doesnt give anything back," correctly reasoning that the function only prints and returns no value, so y is None. This is correct notional-machine reasoning with no catalog misconception.

The student predicts an error because "secret is gone after" the call, correctly reasoning that the local name created inside make() disappears when the call ends, so print(secret) fails. This reflects correct frame-lifetime reasoning, not a catalog misconception.

The student predicted 2 and explained "return stops it," correctly indicating that return ends the call so the print after it never runs. This matches the notional machine with no catalog misconception.

The student says "same list so yeah," correctly treating b = a as binding both names to one shared list object, so b.append(3) shows up in a. This is correct notional-machine reasoning, not a catalog misconception.

The student correctly predicted only "start" prints and justified it with "nobody calls greet," showing they understand the function body does not run merely from the def. This is correct reasoning with no misconception.

The student's explanation "it felt right" does not reveal any reasoning about how the program runs, so it is not informative for identifying misconceptions.

The student only said "i dunno" and did not explain how they think the program runs, so no misconception can be identified.
The student only said "seemed obvious" and did not explain how the program runs, so no misconception can be identified.
The student only says "because that's the answer" and does not explain how the program runs or why `secret` would be available after the call.
